pos: v. (to comfort; to take delight or consolation in)
etymology: Hebrew alas, to rejoice or take delight. Latin solari, to console, giving solatium, comfort. The word is honourable in itself, which is precisely what makes its one biblical occurrence so disturbing.
biblical_def: Come, let us take our fill of love until the morning: let us solace ourselves with loves. This is the speech of the strange woman in Proverbs 7, and the father who records it for his son has chosen to quote her at length rather than merely to warn against her. That is deliberate instruction. The sentence uses the vocabulary of comfort and delight — solace, love — because temptation never presents itself in the language of what it actually is. She speaks of comfort; the chapter has already told us that her house is the way to hell, going down to the chambers of death. The father also tells the son exactly what does the work, and it is not beauty but speech: with her much fair speech she caused him to yield, with the flattering of her lips she forced him. Her mouth is the instrument, as it is at Proverbs 5:3 — the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil. And the sinner's own precaution is quoted too, in the line about her husband: he is not at home, he is gone a long journey. The whole seduction is built on a calculation about who is watching. Scripture's answer throughout is that the calculation is wrong, since the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD, and he pondereth all his goings.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to comfort; to console; to cheer; to amuse; to allay grief or trouble.
webster_full: SOLACE, v.t. To cheer in grief or under calamity; to comfort; to relieve in affliction; to console.
SOLACE, v.t. To allay; to assuage; as, to solace grief.
SOLACE, n. Comfort in grief; alleviation of grief or anxiety; that which relieves in distress.
FLATTERY, n. False praise; commendation bestowed for the purpose of gaining favor and influence.
SEDUCE, v.t. To draw aside or entice from the path of rectitude and duty; to corrupt; to lead astray.
scriptures: Proverbs 7:18
Come, let us take our fill of love until the morning: let us solace ourselves with loves.
Proverbs 7:21
With her much fair speech she caused him to yield, with the flattering of her lips she forced him.
Proverbs 7:27
Her house is the way to hell, going down to the chambers of death.
Proverbs 5:3
For the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil:
corruption_summary: Sexual sin is reframed as the pursuit of intimacy and comfort, which is exactly the vocabulary the tempter uses in this chapter; Proverbs quotes the pitch and then names the destination.
corruption_paragraphs: The strange woman does not say come and commit adultery. She speaks of love, of filling, of solace, and the chapter preserves her words so that a young man will recognise the register when he hears it. The contemporary version is identical in substance: the affair described as a connection, the pornography as a relief from stress, the departure from a covenant as honesty about one's needs. Every one of these is the language of comfort attached to the thing Scripture calls a way to the chambers of death. The dictionary notes that the corruption here is not new and has never needed updating, because it was fully developed when Solomon wrote.

The second observation concerns the instrument, and it cuts against the assumption that lust is chiefly visual. Proverbs says twice that the seduction is verbal — with her much fair speech she caused him to yield, and her mouth is smoother than oil. What ensnares the young man is being spoken to in a way he wants to be spoken to. That is why Scripture's counsel is not merely to look away but to guard the ear and the company, and why the chapter's positive remedy is that the father's own words be bound upon the fingers and written upon the table of the heart. One speech is answered by another.
roots_summary: Hebrew alas (H5965), to rejoice or delight; ravah (H7301), to drink one's fill; zarah (H2114), strange or foreign; chalaq (H2505), smooth or flattering.
roots_lines: Hebrew alas (H5965) — to delight, to take pleasure; rendered solace, its only such rendering.
Hebrew ravah (H7301) — to be saturated, to take one's fill; rendered take our fill.
Hebrew zarah (H2114) — to be strange, foreign; the strange woman of Proverbs.
Hebrew chelqah (H2513) — smoothness, flattery; behind the flattering of her lips.
Hebrew sheol (H7585) — the grave, hell; where the chapter says her house leads.
usage: “let us solace ourselves with loves” — sin speaking the language of comfort.
“with her much fair speech she caused him to yield” — the instrument named.
“her house is the way to hell” — the destination the pitch omits.

pos: n. (a show; something exhibited to be looked at)
etymology: Greek theatron, a theatre, and so what is displayed in one — the root of the English theatre. Latin spectaculum, a show, from spectare, to look at. Paul's image is the arena, where the condemned were brought out last.
biblical_def: For I think that God hath set forth us the apostles last, as it were appointed to death: for we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men. The image is the Roman arena and the detail is exact. The condemned were brought out last, at the end of the day's programme, to die in front of a crowd that had been entertained by everything preceding. Paul says the apostles occupy that slot, and he says God has set them there. The Corinthians were preoccupied with status, with eloquence, with which teacher they belonged to, and Paul answers with a deliberately humiliating comparison in the verses that follow: we are fools for Christ's sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye are strong; ye are honourable, but we are despised. He then drops the irony and simply describes the conditions — even unto this present hour we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace — ending with: we are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day. The word spectacle also reaches further than the human audience. The apostles are a show to angels as well as men, which is the same thought Peter expresses when he says the angels desire to look into these things. What is being publicly exhibited in the sufferings of Christ's servants is watched by more than the crowd in the seats.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a show; something exhibited to view; something presented to the sight or notice, usually of an extraordinary kind.
webster_full: SPECTACLE, n. A show; something exhibited to view; usually, something presented to view as extraordinary, or as worthy of special notice.
SPECTACLE, n. Anything presented to the view, particularly anything that strikes with astonishment.
THEATRE, n. A house or edifice appropriated to the representation of dramatic spectacles; a place of exhibition.
OFFSCOURING, n. That which is scoured off; hence, refuse; recrement; anything vile and despised.
APOSTLE, n. A person deputed to execute some important business; but appropriately, a disciple of Christ commissioned to preach the gospel.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 4:9
For I think that God hath set forth us the apostles last, as it were appointed to death: for we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men.
1 Corinthians 4:10
We are fools for Christ's sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye are strong; ye are honourable, but we are despised.
1 Corinthians 4:11
Even unto this present hour we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace;
1 Corinthians 4:13
Being defamed, we intreat: we are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day.
corruption_summary: Christian ministry is widely modelled on platform, influence, and reputation; Paul locates apostolic ministry in the arena's last slot and says God put it there.
corruption_paragraphs: The celebrity model of ministry — the conference circuit, the personal brand, the platform measured in followers — is the Corinthian error with better technology. That church wanted teachers who reflected well on them, and Paul's response was to describe himself as a condemned man brought out last for the crowd's amusement, hungry, beaten, and homeless. The comparison is not false modesty; it is a direct attack on the metric. A ministry evaluated by reach and reputation is being evaluated by the standard Paul is dismantling, and the New Testament offers no apostle who would have scored well.

The prosperity teaching sharpens the contradiction to a point, since it holds that the King's servants should be visibly prospering and that hardship indicates deficient faith. 1 Corinthians 4 is written by the apostle to the Gentiles about his own settled condition — even unto this present hour — and he attributes the arrangement to God: God hath set forth us the apostles last. The comfort in the passage is real and is available to any faithful servant in obscurity or disgrace. The seats are not the only audience. The spectacle is played before angels, and the verdict that matters is given by the Lord, who Paul says will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the counsels of the hearts.
roots_summary: Greek theatron (G2302), a theatre or spectacle; epithanatios (G1935), appointed to death; perikatharma (G4027), filth or refuse; peripsema (G4067), offscouring.
roots_lines: Greek theatron (G2302) — a theatre, and so a public show; rendered spectacle.
Greek epithanatios (G1935) — condemned to death; rendered appointed to death, its only occurrence.
Greek perikatharma (G4027) — what is scraped off in cleansing; rendered filth of the world.
Greek peripsema (G4067) — scrapings, offscouring; the lowest term Paul could find.
Greek apostolos (G652) — one sent with a commission; the office being described.
usage: “we are made a spectacle unto the world” — the arena's last slot.
“God hath set forth us the apostles last” — the arrangement attributed to God.
“the offscouring of all things” — the lowest word available.

pos: v. (to ponder; to turn a thing over in the mind)
etymology: Hebrew siach, to meditate, to talk with oneself, to rehearse inwardly. The English comes through Old French muser, to loiter or ponder. Scripture's musing is not idle daydreaming but sustained deliberate attention.
biblical_def: I remember the days of old; I meditate on all thy works; I muse on the work of thy hands. Three verbs in one line describe a single discipline, and the order matters. David remembers, which supplies the material; he meditates, which works it over; he muses, which dwells on it. The Hebrew siach carries the sense of talking a thing through with oneself, and the psalm makes clear what the subject is: not the psalmist's feelings, but thy works and the work of thy hands — what God has done. The setting is important too, because this is not a tranquil psalm. David has just said that the enemy hath persecuted my soul; he hath smitten my life down to the ground, and that his spirit is overwhelmed within him. Musing is what he does when he is overwhelmed, and the next line shows what it is for: I stretch forth my hands unto thee: my soul thirsteth after thee, as a thirsty land. Meditation leads into prayer rather than substituting for it. This is the pattern throughout the Psalter — blessed is the man whose delight is in the law of the LORD, and in his law doth he meditate day and night; and, I will meditate also of all thy work, and talk of thy doings. The mind is filled with what God has said and done, and the filling steadies the man.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to ponder; to think closely; to study in silence; to be absent in mind.
webster_full: MUSE, v.i. To ponder; to think closely; to study in silence.
MUSE, v.i. To be absent in mind; to be so occupied in study or contemplation, as not to observe passing scenes or things present.
MUSE, n. Deep thought; close attention; absence of mind.
MEDITATE, v.i. To dwell on any thing in thought; to contemplate; to revolve in the mind.
MEDITATION, n. Close or continued thought; the turning or revolving of a subject in the mind; serious contemplation.
scriptures: Psalm 143:5
I remember the days of old; I meditate on all thy works; I muse on the work of thy hands.
Psalm 143:6
I stretch forth my hands unto thee: my soul thirsteth after thee, as a thirsty land. Selah.
Psalm 1:2
But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.
Psalm 77:12
I will meditate also of all thy work, and talk of thy doings.
corruption_summary: Meditation has been widely redefined as the emptying of the mind, and the biblical practice is confused with techniques whose aim is the opposite of what Scripture commands.
corruption_paragraphs: Eastern meditation aims at emptying — the stilling of thought, the release of attachment, the dissolving of the self — and its vocabulary has been imported wholesale into Western practice, including a good deal of it into churches under the heading of contemplative spirituality. Biblical meditation is the opposite operation. It is filling: I remember, I meditate on all thy works, I muse on the work of thy hands. The object is always something God has said or done, given from outside the meditator, and the faculty engaged is the understanding. A practice that seeks to bypass the mind is not a deeper version of Psalm 143; it is a different activity with a borrowed name.

A second and subtler substitution keeps the Christian vocabulary while changing the object, so that meditation becomes attention to one's own interior states — the examining of feelings, the monitoring of the inner life. There is a place for self-examination and Scripture commands it. But David is overwhelmed, and what he does about it is to turn his mind to what God has done, not to what he himself is experiencing. That is why the psalm moves out of the meditation into prayer and thirst for God, rather than circling back on the psalmist. A man drowning in his own soul is not helped by closer study of the water.
roots_summary: Hebrew siach (H7878), to muse, to talk with oneself; hagah (H1897), to meditate or mutter; zakar (H2142), to remember; maaseh (H4639), a work or deed.
roots_lines: Hebrew siach (H7878) — to ponder, to rehearse inwardly; rendered muse.
Hebrew hagah (H1897) — to murmur, to meditate; rendered meditate at Psalm 1:2.
Hebrew zakar (H2142) — to remember, to call to mind; the first of David's three verbs.
Hebrew maaseh (H4639) — a deed, a work; the object of the meditation.
Hebrew poal (H6467) — work, act; the work of thy hands.
usage: “I muse on the work of thy hands” — the object is what God has done.
“in his law doth he meditate day and night” — the blessed man's habit.
“I stretch forth my hands unto thee” — where the musing leads.

pos: v. (to murmur indistinctly; to speak in a low voice)
etymology: Hebrew hagah, to murmur, to growl, to utter a low sound — the same verb rendered meditate at Psalm 1:2. What distinguishes the two uses is not the sound but the source: the muttering of the medium is set against meditation on the law.
biblical_def: And when they shall say unto you, Seek unto them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep, and that mutter: should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead? Isaiah is describing the ordinary traffic of a nation that has lost confidence in the word of God, and he describes it with contempt for the sound of it. The mediums peep and mutter — chirping and murmuring, the theatrical half-audible voices of the trade. The prophet's reply is two rhetorical questions that dismantle the whole enterprise. Should not a people seek unto their God? — they have a God who speaks plainly and they are consulting substitutes. And for the living to the dead? — the direction of the inquiry is absurd, the living seeking guidance from the dead. Then Isaiah gives the test that settles every such claim, and it is the standing biblical rule for assessing any word purporting to come from God: to the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them. The law had long since closed the door on the practice altogether — regard not them that have familiar spirits, neither seek after wizards, to be defiled by them — and Deuteronomy lists the consulter with familiar spirits, the wizard, and the necromancer among the abominations for which the nations were driven out.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to utter words with a low voice and compressed lips, with sullenness or in complaint; to murmur; to grumble.
webster_full: MUTTER, v.i. To utter words with a low voice and compressed lips, with sullenness or in complaint; to grumble; to murmur.
MUTTER, v.t. To utter with imperfect articulations, or with a low voice.
MUTTERING, ppr. Uttering with a low voice; murmuring.
WIZARD, n. A conjurer; an enchanter; a sorcerer.
NECROMANCY, n. The art of revealing future events by means of a pretended communication with the dead.
scriptures: Isaiah 8:19
And when they shall say unto you, Seek unto them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep, and that mutter: should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?
Isaiah 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Leviticus 19:31
Regard not them that have familiar spirits, neither seek after wizards, to be defiled by them: I am the LORD your God.
Deuteronomy 18:11
Or a charmer, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer.
corruption_summary: Divination is treated as harmless entertainment or as a spiritual practice compatible with faith; Scripture names it as defilement and supplies a plain test for every claimed word from God.
corruption_paragraphs: Consulting the dead and the spirits has never gone away; it has been rebranded. Mediums, psychics, horoscopes, tarot, and the apps that deliver them are the same trade Isaiah describes, and the fact that most participants regard it as amusement changes the practice not at all. Leviticus does not grade it by the sincerity of the enquirer: regard not them that have familiar spirits, neither seek after wizards, to be defiled by them. The defilement attaches to the seeking. And the question Isaiah asks is the one that exposes the absurdity to anyone who has a Bible: a people who possess the speech of the living God are going elsewhere to be muttered at.

Isaiah 8:20 also supplies the test the church needs against a nearer error, since not every claimed revelation comes from a medium. The New Apostolic Reformation and the wider prophetic movement produce a steady stream of words said to be from the Lord, and the biblical rule applies without modification: to the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them. The dictionary holds the closed canon and the cessation of the revelatory gifts, and notes that the test Isaiah gives would be sufficient even for those who do not: a word that cannot be checked against Scripture is not to be received, whatever voice delivers it.
roots_summary: Hebrew hagah (H1897), to murmur or mutter; ob (H178), a familiar spirit; yiddeoni (H3049), a wizard or knowing one; tsaphaph (H6850), to chirp or peep.
roots_lines: Hebrew hagah (H1897) — to murmur, to growl; rendered mutter here and meditate at Psalm 1:2.
Hebrew ob (H178) — a familiar spirit, or the medium who has one; the word used of the witch of Endor.
Hebrew yiddeoni (H3049) — a knowing one, a wizard; always paired with ob in the prohibitions.
Hebrew tsaphaph (H6850) — to chirp as a bird; rendered peep, of the medium's voice.
Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, instruction; the first half of the test at Isaiah 8:20.
usage: “wizards that peep, and that mutter” — the theatrical voices of the trade.
“for the living to the dead?” — the absurdity of the direction.
“to the law and to the testimony” — the test for every claimed word.

pos: v. (slipped back; fallen away by degrees)
etymology: Hebrew shobeb, turned back, apostate, from shub, to turn — the same root that gives the word for return and repent. The Authorized Version's slidden back catches the gradualness: not a leap but a slipping.
biblical_def: Why then is this people of Jerusalem slidden back by a perpetual backsliding? they hold fast deceit, they refuse to return. The image is of ground giving way underfoot, and the adjective is the terrible part: a perpetual backsliding, a slipping that has become the settled direction of travel. Jeremiah then names two things that hold it in place, and both are acts of the will. They hold fast deceit — the grip is deliberate, and what is gripped is a lie. They refuse to return — the door is open and they will not go through it. That second clause is decisive, because backsliding in Scripture is never presented as a misfortune that overtakes a passive man. The Hebrew root behind slidden is the same root as return: the backslider is a man who has turned away and will not turn back, and the remedy is named in the same vocabulary as the disease. The prophet describes the mechanism in the next verse with painful accuracy: no man repented him of his wickedness, saying, What have I done? every one turned to his course, as the horse rusheth into the battle. And yet the word that stands over the whole is an invitation, not a dismissal. Return, ye backsliding children, and I will heal your backslidings; and, I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), under SLIDE and BACKSLIDE: to slip; to move or slip backwards; to fall off gradually; to apostatize.
webster_full: SLIDDEN, pp. of slide. Slipped; moved along a smooth surface; fallen.
BACKSLIDE, v.i. To fall off; to apostatize; to turn gradually from the faith and practice of Christianity.
BACKSLIDER, n. An apostate; one who falls from the faith and practice of religion.
BACKSLIDING, n. The act of apostatizing from faith or practice; a falling insensibly from religion.
DECEIT, n. Fraud; fallacy; cheat; any declaration, artifice or practice which misleads another.
scriptures: Jeremiah 8:5
Why then is this people of Jerusalem slidden back by a perpetual backsliding? they hold fast deceit, they refuse to return.
Jeremiah 8:6
I hearkened and heard, but they spake not aright: no man repented him of his wickedness, saying, What have I done? every one turned to his course, as the horse rusheth into the battle.
Jeremiah 3:22
Return, ye backsliding children, and I will heal your backslidings. Behold, we come unto thee; for thou art the LORD our God.
Hosea 14:4
I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely: for mine anger is turned away from him.
corruption_summary: Backsliding is explained as burnout or a season of doubt, which removes the will from the account; Jeremiah traces it to holding fast deceit and refusing to return, and the remedy offered is repentance and free healing.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic account of falling away speaks of exhaustion, deconstruction, or a natural season of questioning, and each of these describes something real. But they share a feature that Jeremiah's account does not have: the man in them is passive, and things happen to him. The prophet says they hold fast deceit, they refuse to return — two verbs of the will, one gripping and one refusing. That diagnosis is harder and also more hopeful, because a refusal can be reversed and a drift cannot. Where the will is removed from the account, so is the possibility of repentance, and all that remains is to explain the departure sympathetically.

The opposite hardness treats every backslider as certainly reprobate and closes the door Scripture leaves open. Jeremiah's own book, in the middle of the indictment, records the call: Return, ye backsliding children, and I will heal your backslidings. Hosea goes further — I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely. The dictionary holds the perseverance of the saints, and therefore holds that those who finally and permanently depart give evidence they were never Christ's. It also holds that no one in this life can read that verdict off a man's present condition, and that the church's word to anyone still within reach of it is the prophet's word: return.
roots_summary: Hebrew shobeb (H7728), backsliding or apostate; shub (H7725), to turn, to return, to repent; meshubah (H4878), backsliding; tarmith (H8649), deceit.
roots_lines: Hebrew shobeb (H7728) — turned away, backsliding; rendered slidden back.
Hebrew shub (H7725) — to turn back, to return; the root of both the disease and the cure.
Hebrew meshubah (H4878) — a turning away, backsliding; what God promises to heal.
Hebrew tarmith (H8649) — deceit, fraud; what the people hold fast.
Hebrew maen (H3985) — to refuse; they refuse to return, the act of the will.
usage: “slidden back by a perpetual backsliding” — a slip become a direction.
“they hold fast deceit, they refuse to return” — two verbs of the will.
“I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely” — the open door.

pos: adj. (hard of heart; unyielding in will)
etymology: Hebrew chazaq leb, strong or hard of heart — the same verb used of Pharaoh's hardening. The Authorized Version's compound pairs it with impudent, literally hard of face, so that the prophet is sent to people hard in both the face they show and the heart behind it.
biblical_def: For they are impudent children and stiffhearted. I do send thee unto them; and thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD. The commissioning of Ezekiel is unlike any other in Scripture for its candour about the outcome. God tells the prophet in advance that his hearers are hard, and the two words are a matched pair — impudent is literally hard of face, stiffhearted is hard of heart. Hard outside and hard within. Then comes the sentence that has steadied preachers ever since: I do send thee unto them, followed by the words he is to say, Thus saith the Lord GOD. The commission is not withdrawn because the ground is bad. God is explicit that the message will be refused — the house of Israel will not hearken unto thee; for they will not hearken unto me — and equally explicit that it must still be delivered: whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear. The prophet's success is defined by faithfulness in speaking, not by response in hearing. And God supplies what the task requires rather than removing the task: behold, I have made thy face strong against their faces, and thy forehead strong against their foreheads. The hardness is answered with a God-given firmness of the same kind, which is the only realistic provision for a man sent to people like this.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), under STIFF and HEARTED: obstinate; stubborn; not yielding to argument or persuasion; hard-hearted.
webster_full: STIFFHEARTED, a. Obstinate; stubborn; contumacious.
STIFF, a. Not easily bent; rigid; not flexible; stubborn; not easily subdued or persuaded.
IMPUDENT, a. Shameless; wanting modesty; bold with contempt of others; saucy.
OBSTINATE, a. Stubborn; fixed firmly in resolution or purpose; not yielding to reason, arguments or other means.
HARDNESS, n. Obduracy; impenitence; confirmed state of wickedness.
scriptures: Ezekiel 2:4
For they are impudent children and stiffhearted. I do send thee unto them; and thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD.
Ezekiel 2:5
And they, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear, (for they are a rebellious house,) yet shall know that there hath been a prophet among them.
Ezekiel 3:7
But the house of Israel will not hearken unto thee; for they will not hearken unto me: for all the house of Israel are impudent and hardhearted.
Ezekiel 3:8
Behold, I have made thy face strong against their faces, and thy forehead strong against their foreheads.
corruption_summary: Ministry is now widely evaluated by response, so that resistance is read as a failure of method; Ezekiel is told the response in advance and sent anyway, with faithfulness defined as speaking.
corruption_paragraphs: Where the effectiveness of preaching is measured by visible result, a congregation that does not respond becomes evidence that the preacher must change something — his tone, his approach, his emphasis. The pragmatic instinct then does what it always does and adjusts the message until the response improves. Ezekiel 2 forecloses the reasoning at the outset. God names the hardness, predicts the refusal, and commissions the prophet in the same breath, giving as the measure of the mission not conversion but this: yet shall know that there hath been a prophet among them. A faithful man may labour among stiffhearted people for a lifetime and have discharged his commission exactly.

The passage cuts the other way as well, against a hardness the preacher himself may acquire. God does not tell Ezekiel to become contemptuous of his hearers; he makes the prophet's forehead strong, which is endurance rather than scorn, and the same prophet is later shown weeping and sitting astonished among the captives seven days. A minister who has learned to expect resistance is in danger of welcoming it as proof of his soundness, and of mistaking a hard manner for a strong forehead. The Lord looked on a city that would not receive him and wept over it, having already pronounced its judgment. Both belong together.
roots_summary: Hebrew chazaq (H2389), strong, hard; leb (H3820), heart; qasheh (H7186), stiff, stubborn; metsach (H4696), forehead.
roots_lines: Hebrew chazaq leb (H2389, H3820) — hard of heart; rendered stiffhearted.
Hebrew qasheh (H7186) — hard, stiff, severe; the root behind stiffnecked throughout the Pentateuch.
Hebrew metsach (H4696) — forehead, brow; hard in them, made strong in the prophet.
Hebrew panim (H6440) — face; impudent is literally hard of face.
Hebrew mariy (H4805) — rebellion; a rebellious house, the standing description in Ezekiel.
usage: “impudent children and stiffhearted” — hard in face and heart alike.
“I do send thee unto them” — the commission given with the warning.
“I have made thy face strong against their faces” — the provision, not the exemption.

pos: n. (an instant; the time of a blink)
etymology: Greek rhipe, a throw, a jerk, a rapid movement — here of the eye, and so the briefest measurable interval. The English twinkle is Old English twinclian, to blink or wink.
biblical_def: In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed. Paul is describing the resurrection of the body at the return of Christ, and he chooses the shortest unit of time the language had. Rhipe is a flick or a dart of movement; joined to the eye it means a blink. Two things are asserted about the change and both are absolute. It is instantaneous — not a process of purification, not a gradual refinement, but a change accomplished in the interval of a blink. And it is universal among God's people: we shall be changed, the living along with the raised dead. Paul gives the reason in the verse following: for this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality. The resurrection body is not the old body repaired; it is the same body raised imperishable, which is why he says put on rather than exchange. The event is fixed to a public signal, at the last trump, and Paul describes the same moment to the Thessalonians: the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first. And the transformation is Christ's own work on the believer's body: who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a shutting and opening of the eye; a wink; hence, a moment; an instant.
webster_full: TWINKLING, n. A shutting and opening of the eye; a wink.
TWINKLING, n. A moment; an instant; the time of a wink.
TWINKLE, v.i. To open and shut the eye rapidly; to wink.
MOMENT, n. The most minute and indivisible part of time; an instant.
INCORRUPTIBLE, a. That cannot corrupt or decay; not admitting of corruption.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 15:52
In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.
1 Corinthians 15:53
For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.
1 Thessalonians 4:16
For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first:
Philippians 3:21
Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself.
corruption_summary: The bodily resurrection is spiritualised into the survival of the soul, or fragmented by schemes that multiply the returns of Christ; Paul describes one public trumpet and one instantaneous change.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest corruption is not a denial but a substitution: the resurrection quietly replaced by the immortality of the soul, so that the Christian hope becomes going to heaven when one dies and the body is left out entirely. Paul will not have it. His subject throughout 1 Corinthians 15 is the body — sown in corruption, raised in incorruption; this corruptible, this mortal. The intermediate state is real and blessed, and to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord; but it is not the hope. The hope is the bodily resurrection at the last trump, and the creeds confess exactly that.

The dispensational scheme divides the event Paul presents as one. A secret rapture separated from the visible return by a period of years requires two comings and two trumpets, and this verse names a last trump, which is difficult to place before a later one. Paul's parallel in 1 Thessalonians describes a descent with a shout, the voice of an archangel, and the trump of God — nothing about it is secret. The system is a nineteenth-century development from Darby and Scofield and appears in no Reformation confession. The dictionary holds one bodily second coming, at which the dead in Christ are raised and the living changed, in the twinkling of an eye.
roots_summary: Greek rhipe (G4493), a rapid movement or blink; atomos (G823), indivisible, a moment; salpigx (G4536), a trumpet; aphtharsia (G861), incorruption.
roots_lines: Greek rhipe (G4493) — a jerk, a flick; rendered twinkling, its only occurrence.
Greek atomos (G823) — uncut, indivisible; rendered a moment, its only occurrence.
Greek salpigx (G4536) — a trumpet; the last trump, a public signal.
Greek aphtharsia (G861) — incorruption; what the corruptible must put on.
Greek allasso (G236) — to change; we shall be changed.
usage: “in the twinkling of an eye” — the shortest unit the language had.
“this corruptible must put on incorruption” — the same body, raised.
“the dead in Christ shall rise first” — the same moment in Thessalonians.

pos: n. (the standing of a surety; the assuming of another's debt)
etymology: Hebrew taqa, to strike, as in striking hands to seal a pledge — the gesture that bound a man to another's debt. Latin securitas, through Old French surte: the condition of one who stands security for another.
biblical_def: He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it: and he that hateth suretiship is sure. A surety is a man who makes himself liable for another's debt, and the wisdom literature returns to the practice repeatedly with the same counsel: do not do it. Proverbs is not condemning generosity — it commands giving throughout — but a specific arrangement in which a man pledges his own solvency against an obligation he does not control. The warnings are urgent and practical: be not thou one of them that strike hands, or of them that are sureties for debts; if thou hast nothing to pay, why should he take away thy bed from under thee? And, a man void of understanding striketh hands, and becometh surety in the presence of his friend. The reason is plain enough. The surety carries all the risk and none of the decisions, and the man who has accepted such a position may find his household ruined by another man's choices. There is a striking exception, and Scripture builds its greatest doctrine on it. Hebrews says of Christ, By so much was Jesus made a surety of a better testament. He did exactly what Proverbs warns a man not to do — assumed liability for debtors who could not pay, with full knowledge of the cost — and the thing Proverbs says will make a man smart is precisely what happened at the cross.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the state of being surety; the obligation of a person to answer for another and make good any debt or loss which may arise from another's delinquency.
webster_full: SURETISHIP, n. The state of being surety; the obligation of a person to answer for another, and to make good any debt or loss which may occur from another's delinquency.
SURETY, n. One that is bound with and for another; one who enters into a bond or recognizance to answer for another's appearance, or for his payment of a debt.
SURETY, n. Security; safety; certainty; indubitableness.
BOND, n. An obligation or deed by which a person binds himself, his heirs, executors and administrators, to pay a certain sum on or before a future day appointed.
SMART, v.i. To feel a lively pungent pain; to bear a penalty or the evil consequences of any thing.
scriptures: Proverbs 11:15
He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it: and he that hateth suretiship is sure.
Proverbs 22:26
Be not thou one of them that strike hands, or of them that are sureties for debts.
Proverbs 17:18
A man void of understanding striketh hands, and becometh surety in the presence of his friend.
Hebrews 7:22
By so much was Jesus made a surety of a better testament.
corruption_summary: Proverbs' counsel is read either as a general endorsement of financial self-protection or dismissed as ancient advice; and the doctrine it prepares — Christ as surety — is weakened wherever the atonement is made less than substitutionary.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the turning of prudential wisdom into a principle of self-protection that overrides plain commands. Proverbs warns against assuming liability for debts a man cannot control; it nowhere teaches him to keep his money safe from his brother's need. The same book commands giving to the poor, and the New Testament commands bearing one another's burdens. Wisdom literature gives counsel for the ordinary case, and a Christian who cites Proverbs 11:15 to avoid sacrificial generosity has quoted the right verse for the wrong purpose.

The doctrinal weight of the word lies in Hebrews 7:22, and it is lost wherever the atonement is made something less than substitution. If the cross is chiefly a demonstration of love, or an example of self-giving, or a victory over powers with no debt actually transferred, then surety is a metaphor with nothing behind it. Scripture means it legally. Christ stood in the place of debtors, assumed an obligation that was not his, and discharged it in his own body — which is why Proverbs' warning is so illuminating by contrast. What is folly for a man void of understanding was, for the Son of God, deliberate, costly, and undertaken with full knowledge of the price.
roots_summary: Hebrew taqa (H8628), to strike, as hands in pledge; arab (H6148), to become surety; zur (H2114), a stranger; Greek egguos (G1450), a surety.
roots_lines: Hebrew taqa (H8628) — to strike, as striking hands to seal a pledge; behind suretiship.
Hebrew arab (H6148) — to give in pledge, to become surety for another.
Hebrew zur (H2114) — a stranger; the one for whom suretiship is most dangerous.
Hebrew raa (H7489) — to be broken, to suffer hurt; rendered shall smart for it.
Greek egguos (G1450) — a surety, one who gives security; used of Jesus at Hebrews 7:22, its only occurrence.
usage: “he that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it” — the prudential warning.
“be not thou one of them that strike hands” — the gesture that bound a man.
“Jesus made a surety of a better testament” — the one who did it knowingly.

pos: adj. (not keeping in mind; heedless; forgetful)
etymology: Hebrew shakach, to forget, in a form meaning to be neglectful of. The English compounds un- with mindful: not holding in mind. Moses pairs it with the plainer verb in the same line — unmindful, and hast forgotten.
biblical_def: Of the Rock that begat thee thou art unmindful, and hast forgotten God that formed thee. The Song of Moses is a covenant lawsuit set to music, and this line states the charge. Israel's sin is described not as ignorance but as forgetting — the loss of a thing once known and possessed. Two divine titles carry the indictment. God is the Rock that begat thee and God that formed thee; both are titles of origin, and to forget them is to forget where one came from. Moses has already made the argument that should have made forgetting impossible: do ye thus requite the LORD, O foolish people and unwise? is not he thy father that hath bought thee? hath he not made thee, and established thee? The mechanism of the forgetting is given a few lines earlier and it is not hardship but prosperity: Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked; then he forsook God which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation. This is the pattern Deuteronomy warns about at length — that a full belly, good houses, and multiplied herds are the conditions under which a people most readily forgets the God who gave them. Isaiah levels the same charge against a later generation in almost the same words: thou hast forgotten the LORD thy maker, that hath stretched forth the heavens, and laid the foundations of the earth.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): not mindful; not heedful; regardless; negligent; careless; inattentive.
webster_full: UNMINDFUL, a. Not mindful; not heedful; regardless; negligent; careless.
MINDFUL, a. Attentive; regarding with care; bearing in mind; heedful; observant.
FORGET, v.t. To lose the remembrance of; to let go from the memory; to slight; to neglect.
ROCK, n. A defense; means of safety; protection; strength; an asylum; applied to God.
UNGRATEFUL, a. Not thankful for favors; making no returns or making ill returns for kindness.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 32:18
Of the Rock that begat thee thou art unmindful, and hast forgotten God that formed thee.
Deuteronomy 32:15
But Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked: thou art waxen fat, thou art grown thick, thou art covered with fatness; then he forsook God which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation.
Deuteronomy 32:6
Do ye thus requite the LORD, O foolish people and unwise? is not he thy father that hath bought thee? hath he not made thee, and established thee?
Isaiah 51:13

And forgettest the LORD thy maker, that hath stretched forth the heavens, and laid the foundations of the earth; and hast feared continually every day because of the fury of the oppressor, as if he were ready to destroy; and where is the oppressor?
corruption_summary: Forgetting God is treated as a private lapse of devotion; Moses presents it as covenant treachery, and names prosperity rather than suffering as the condition that produces it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is uncontested and the principle to recover is the one the Song insists on: the direction from which apostasy usually comes. Christians are trained to watch for the dangers of affliction, and Scripture does warn of them. But Deuteronomy 32 puts the fall after the feast — Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked — and the whole book repeats the warning that when Israel has eaten and is full and has built goodly houses, then the heart will be lifted up and the LORD forgotten. A comfortable church is in the circumstance Moses treats as most dangerous, and it will not feel dangerous, which is the difficulty.

The second matter is what forgetting actually means here. It is not a failure of recall; Israel could recite the history. It is the practical dropping out of God from the way a people reckons its life — decisions made, wealth accumulated, and futures planned as though the Rock that begat them were not a live factor. Isaiah's version of the charge makes the cost vivid by pairing it with fear: forgettest the LORD thy maker, and hast feared continually every day because of the fury of the oppressor. A man who forgets God does not thereby become free of fear; he simply transfers it to something smaller.
roots_summary: Hebrew shakach (H7911), to forget; tsur (H6697), a rock; yalad (H3205), to beget; chul (H2342), to bring forth or form.
roots_lines: Hebrew shakach (H7911) — to forget, to neglect; rendered both unmindful and hast forgotten.
Hebrew tsur (H6697) — a rock, a cliff; a standing divine title in the Song of Moses.
Hebrew yalad (H3205) — to beget, to bear; the Rock that begat thee.
Hebrew chul (H2342) — to writhe, to bring forth; behind God that formed thee.
Hebrew Yeshurun (H3484) — the upright one, a poetic name for Israel; who waxed fat and kicked.
usage: “of the Rock that begat thee thou art unmindful” — forgetting one's origin.
“Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked” — the condition that produced it.
“is not he thy father that hath bought thee?” — the argument against forgetting.

etymology: Greek apeiros, from a-, without, and peira, trial or experience — untried, inexperienced. The English unskilful in its older sense means lacking practised competence, not clumsy.
biblical_def: For every one that useth milk is unskilful in the word of righteousness: for he is a babe. The writer to the Hebrews is rebuking a congregation that should have progressed and has not: for when for the time ye ought to be teachers, ye have need that one teach you again which be the first principles of the oracles of God. The problem is not that they are young in the faith but that they are old in it and still on milk. Apeiros means untried — without experience — and the diagnosis is about practised judgment rather than information. The next verse makes this explicit and gives the remedy: but strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil. Three words there carry the argument. Use — the thing must be practised. Exercised is a term from the gymnasium, the training of an athlete. And what is developed is the capacity to discern. Maturity in Scripture is therefore not the accumulation of doctrine but the trained ability to apply it, and it is gained the way any skill is gained, by repeated exercise under the word. The writer's conclusion is an instruction to move: therefore leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): wanting skill or knowledge; inexperienced; wanting art; unacquainted.
webster_full: UNSKILFUL, a. Wanting skill; wanting the knowledge and dexterity which practice confers.
UNSKILFUL, a. Unacquainted; not knowing; inexperienced.
SKILL, n. The familiar knowledge of any art or science, united with readiness and dexterity in execution or performance.
EXERCISE, v.t. To exert the body or mind for the sake of improvement; to train by use.
DISCERN, v.t. To distinguish; to see the difference between two or more things; to judge.
scriptures: Hebrews 5:13
For every one that useth milk is unskilful in the word of righteousness: for he is a babe.
Hebrews 5:12

For when for the time ye ought to be teachers, ye have need that one teach you again which be the first principles of the oracles of God; and are become such as have need of milk, and not of strong meat.
Hebrews 5:14
But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.
1 Peter 2:2
As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby:
corruption_summary: Spiritual maturity is measured by information held or by length of profession; Hebrews measures it by trained discernment, gained through exercise, and treats prolonged infancy as a rebuke.
corruption_paragraphs: Two false measures of maturity are common. The first counts knowledge: a believer who can state the doctrines accurately is assumed to be mature, though he may never have had to apply one of them under pressure. The second counts years: long attendance is taken for growth. Hebrews measures neither. Its standard is senses exercised to discern both good and evil — a trained faculty, acquired by reason of use, in the way a soldier or an athlete acquires competence. Doctrine is the food and discernment is the strength it is supposed to produce, and a man may eat without ever getting up.

The other side of the rebuke falls on how churches teach. A congregation kept indefinitely on first principles, because deeper teaching is thought to be beyond the people or bad for attendance, is being maintained in the condition this passage calls a fault. The writer does not respond to immaturity by simplifying further; he says let us go on unto perfection and proceeds to the hardest argument in the letter. Peter's command that newborn babes desire the sincere milk of the word is not in tension with this. Milk is right for the newborn and wrong for the man who has been at the table for years.
